{{short description|Logical fallacy equating naming something with explaining it}}
The '''nominal fallacy''', also known as the '''naming-explaining fallacy''', is a [[logical fallacy]] in which it is incorrectly assumed that giving something a name is tantamount to explaining it.<ref>{{Cite encyclopedia |title=Nominal Fallacy |encyclopedia=Encyclopedia of Animal Cognition and Behavior |publisher=Springer International Publishing |location=Cham |url=http://link.springer.com/10.1007/978-3-319-47829-6_357-1 |last=Remedios |first=Richard |date=2018 |pages=1–2 |language=en |doi=10.1007/978-3-319-47829-6_357-1 |isbn=978-3-319-47829-6|url-access=subscription }}</ref> [[Stuart Firestein]] has described the fallacy as "...the error of believing that the label carries explanatory information."<ref name="firestein">{{Cite web |url=https://www.edge.org/response-detail/11730 |title=What scientific concept would improve everybody's cognitive toolkit? |last=Firestein |first=Stuart |date=2011 |website=Edge.org |access-date=2020-01-03}}</ref> One example of the nominal fallacy is the use of the word "[[instinct]]" to explain a given behavior.<ref name="firestein"/>
An assertion, statement or assumption that an entity X exhibits a certain property due to its name would exemplify the nominal fallacy.
